# Getting Started

Babqua is currently developed and tested on Linux. macOS hasn't been
verified — if you try it, please
[open an issue](https://github.com/scicloj/babqua/issues) with what
you find.

## Prerequisites

1. **[Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/)** — the
   publishing system
2. **[Babashka](https://github.com/babashka/babashka#installation)** —
   the Clojure scripting runtime

That's the whole list. No JVM, no `bbin`, no nREPL client to install.

Verify both are available:

```bash
quarto --version
bb --version
```

## Create a project

```bash
mkdir my-bb-doc
cd my-bb-doc
```

If you want to bring in extra libraries or
[pods](https://github.com/babashka/babashka/blob/master/doc/projects.md#pods)
later, drop a `bb.edn` here — Babashka auto-loads it from the
directory it runs in, so notebook code blocks see the same deps and
pods you'd see from a regular bb script.

## Install the extension

Run this **inside your project directory** — it creates an
`_extensions/` folder there:

```bash
quarto add scicloj/babqua
```

Sanity check that the filter files landed:

```bash
ls _extensions/scicloj/bb/
```

You should see `babqua.lua`, `runtime.bb`, `babqua.css`, and
`_extension.yml`.

## Write a document

Create a file called `hello.qmd`:

````markdown
---
title: "Hello Babashka"
filters:
  - bb
---

```{.clojure .bb}
(+ 1 2 3)
```

```{.clojure .bb}
^:kind/hiccup
[:div {:style "color: coral; font-size: 24px;"} "Hello from Babashka!"]
```
````

Note the `{.clojure .bb}` syntax: `.clojure` enables syntax
highlighting (in editors and rendered output), and `.bb` tells the
Babqua filter to evaluate the block. Both use dot prefixes — that's
[Pandoc class syntax](https://pandoc.org/MANUAL.html#divs-and-spans).

The `filters: [bb]` in the
[frontmatter](https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/front-matter.html)
(the YAML header at the top of the file, between the `---` markers)
tells Quarto to use the Babqua filter.

## Render it

```bash
quarto render hello.qmd
```

This launches a single Babashka process, evaluates the code blocks in
order, and produces `hello.html`. Babashka's startup cost is small
enough (tens of milliseconds) that there's no persistent process to
manage — each render is fresh.
